scope.quote:
We analyze a procedure common in empirical accounting and finance re
 search where researchers use ordinary least squares to decompose a depen
 dent variable into its predicted and residual components and use the residu
 als as the dependent variable in a second regression. This two-step procedure
 is used to examine determinants of constructs such as discretionary accru
 als, real activities management, discretionary book-tax differences, and abnor
 mal investment. We show that the typical implementation of this procedure
 generates biased coefficients and standard errors that can lead to incorrect
 inferences, with both Type I and Type II errors. We further show that the
 magnitude of the bias in coefficients and standard errors is a function of the
 correlations between model regressors. We illustrate the potential magnitude
 of the bias in accounting research in four commonly used settings.

We use the Frisch-Waugh-Lovell Theorem and simulations to demon
 strate that this two-step procedure produces biased coefficients and
 f-statistics.

To more directly illustrate the possible effects of the two-step regression
 procedure in accounting research, we examine several settings where this
 approach is used. Specifically, we consider the consequences of the two
 step procedure in evaluating proposed determinants of (1) discretionary
 accruals, (2) discretionary expenditures (i.e., real activities management),
 (3) discretionary permanent book-tax differences (i.e., tax aggressiveness),
 and (4) abnormal investment. In each of these settings we estimate coeffi
 cients and /-statistics using single-step regressions and compare the results
 with those obtained from two-step regressions. We do this for several vari
 ables of interest and with different combinations of second-step control
 variables.

scope.quote:
We analyze a procedure common in empirical accounting and finance re
 search where researchers use ordinary least squares to decompose a depen
 dent variable into its predicted and residual components and use the residu
 als as the dependent variable in a second regression. This two-step procedure
 is used to examine determinants of constructs such as discretionary accru
 als, real activities management, discretionary book-tax differences, and abnor
 mal investment. We show that the typical implementation of this procedure
 generates biased coefficients and standard errors that can lead to incorrect
 inferences, with both Type I and Type II errors. We further show that the
 magnitude of the bias in coefficients and standard errors is a function of the
 correlations between model regressors. We illustrate the potential magnitude
 of the bias in accounting research in four commonly used settings.

We use the Frisch-Waugh-Lovell Theorem and simulations to demon
 strate that this two-step procedure produces biased coefficients and
 f-statistics.

To more directly illustrate the possible effects of the two-step regression
 procedure in accounting research, we examine several settings where this
 approach is used. Specifically, we consider the consequences of the two
 step procedure in evaluating proposed determinants of (1) discretionary
 accruals, (2) discretionary expenditures (i.e., real activities management),
 (3) discretionary permanent book-tax differences (i.e., tax aggressiveness),
 and (4) abnormal investment. In each of these settings we estimate coeffi
 cients and /-statistics using single-step regressions and compare the results
 with those obtained from two-step regressions. We do this for several vari
 ables of interest and with different combinations of second-step control
 variables.

Source-first correction: the paper’s principal contribution is methodological. The abstract and introduction identify bias in the common two-step residual regression and use Frisch–Waugh–Lovell analysis and simulations to establish the result. Retain the actually fitted Monte Carlo full-model and standard two-step regressions underlying Tables 3–4; retain the first stage as the residual construction required by the second stage.

Do not treat Table 2 as a regression result: its bias grids are analytically derived; the simulation reported in the text verifies those formulas but is untabulated. Section 4/Table 5 is an accounting application used to illustrate the method, after the method/simulation contribution, and is outside this selected family. The three equations in the simulation comparison are one full OLS fit, the two-step first-stage fit, and its residual second-stage fit.

The previous Table 5 scope relied on matching sample metadata to choose a family; that was not used for this source-first correction. The sample record links to the later Compustat application and does not establish the principal method family.
